extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for novelists on planning, weaving, and resolving subplots (recast as 'story strands') so they pace the book, build tension, and reinforce themes without becoming irrelevant or confusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think of subplots as story strands
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplots should be treated as story strands that intertwine with the main storyline rather than separate, inferior stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article prefers the term 'story strands' because different strands 'intertwine with the main one, building it up from a single strand into a fascinating, deeply textured plot.' Avoid the anti-pattern of adding a 'completely irrelevant subplot' (e.g., a lost cat or a child’s birthday) that slows the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strands to pace the story and keep tension rising
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplots help pace your story and keep the tension rising when used intentionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ strands at different stages to maintain momentum; moving from one strand to another or when strands collide can create twists. Avoid inserting a subplot merely because 'there's not enough going on'—that tends to slow action rather than sustain tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match number of strands to the length/scale of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriate number of story strands depends on the length of the work: short pieces usually need one, longer novels can support multiple strands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short stories and picture books typically have a single linear plot. Longer novels can include more strands; example: the author's 7,000-word Pony-Mad Princess books usually have two strands and she 'always aim[s] to end both strands in the final chapter.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow prominence of strands to shift across the book
rubrics_metrics.description: Different strands will be more important at various stages; prominence can shift and that movement can drive twists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As in a plait, different strands become the 'top one' as you work; use those shifts intentionally to carry the reader forward and to create surprising turns when strands collide or trade focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve strands carefully; avoid loose or untidy strands
rubrics_metrics.description: Some strands should be resolved with the main storyline, others during the course of the book, but avoid leaving strands that 'fizzle out' or go nowhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns against 'an untidy plait with lots of straggly bits sticking out the sides' and notes readers dislike strands that 'go nowhere.' Decide which strands will conclude at the main resolution and which will resolve earlier, and handle those resolutions with care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mirrored/complementary strands to reinforce theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Design strands that complement or mirror each other to strengthen thematic resonance and character arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in There Must Be Horses, one strand (a girl's inability to trust) mirrors a horse's inability to trust; as they weave together they heal each other. Mirrored strands can create satisfying thematic and emotional payoff when woven together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use initially unconnected strands that later join (if appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: You may present separate strands that appear unrelated at first and link them later to build suspense and reader expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disaster stories or thrillers you can introduce multiple characters in different situations and bring them together via a big event. Experienced readers will expect a link, so 'hint at possibilities' and build tension about when and how the connection will be revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce strands/characters strategically to maintain reader attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Control when you introduce other strands or characters so readers know whom to care about and are not pulled in too many directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you jump between characters too much readers may be unsure which one to care about. Techniques: introduce one character first and only add others when their strands meet; or concentrate on one strand until a pivotal event (e.g., focus on the girl until she's murdered, then introduce the detective's strand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weave strands deliberately using step outlines or visual aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan and experiment with the order and intersection of strand beats to create a coherent multi-stranded plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a step outline for each strand, put each step on separate sticky notes and use different colors for each strand, then move the pieces around to try different joins. The goal is 'a single, multi-colored line of sticky notes' that shows how strands interlock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay flexible in plotting; let a strong strand become the main storyline
rubrics_metrics.description: During plotting, be willing to swap which strand is the main storyline if another strand resonates more strongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main storyline is mutable at the plotting stage; if a secondary strand begins to 'take over' follow your instincts and swap them—it's easy at this stage and can be swapped back later if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be able to identify the main storyline (elevator pitch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Know which strand is your core story—the one you'd describe in a single sentence or an 'elevator pitch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main storyline is 'the one you would talk about if you were asked to describe your book in one sentence.' Use that clarity to guide plotting and decisions about which strands resolve when.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive switching that fragments reader focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Too-frequent jumps between strands can make it hard for readers to care or follow; manage rhythm and transitions carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you 'jump around between strands' so much readers are unsure whom to care about, reduce switching or restructure introductions/timing so emotional investment is maintained.
